current_episode.title: A personal touch: elevating safety compliance through technology and leadership

guest.entreprise_secondaire: Safety software company (acquired by KPA services)
guest.bio_context: Darren Boyd started his career at the University of Oklahoma as director of basketball operations for the women's basketball team, working with the coaching staff for six or seven seasons. He then transitioned to athletics development as an assistant athletics director focused on fundraising and donor relations for five to six years. In 2011, he joined an oilfield services water transfer company on the operations side and was promoted to oversee the health and safety department within 90 days. This experience managing safety compliance across 1,200 employees in 24 US locations led him to co-found a safety software company in 2014 with two partners, which was later acquired by KPA services, where he now leads new market expansion and product development.

pending_qa.q: What specific problem did Boyd's software address in field auditing and reporting?
pending_qa.r: Field auditors had to drive to job sites, spend two to three hours performing audits, drive back, and type up reports at night with pictures and notes, creating a gap of time before reports reached leadership. Boyd's software enables real-time field reporting with automatic photo uploads and instant distribution to leadership, allowing issues to be addressed immediately and giving employees work-life balance by keeping them off desks after hours.

pending_qa.q: What is the importance of behavior-based safety and rapid employee feedback in Boyd's philosophy?
pending_qa.r: Boyd implemented behavior-based safety where all employees report observations they find concerning. The most damaging thing to safety culture is crickets, meaning no feedback. When employees report concerns and receive rapid response from leadership, managers, and resources within minutes, it strengthens team culture and trust. Slow or no response turns employees away from reporting.

pending_qa.q: What is an example of the real-world safety issue Boyd's software helped address?
pending_qa.r: In South Texas, employees observed rattlesnakes nesting under warm black poly pipeline during cold weather. An employee submitted an observation card on paper, but it took five weeks to reach Boyd, and by then the employee had left the company and no action was taken. This demonstrated why digital, real-time reporting systems are essential to capture and act on safety concerns immediately.

pending_qa.q: What are the risks Boyd identifies with over-automation in safety processes?
pending_qa.r: Boyd warns against letting artificial intelligence control pre-job safety meetings, which some companies attempt. He believes you need the actual conversation to happen—employees discussing what they will do, who does what task, what could hurt them, and confirming everyone is trained and has required PPE. Pushing a button on a mobile app cannot replace the in-person dialogue required for effective safety culture.

pending_qa.q: How does Darren Boyd draw parallels between sports and safety leadership?
pending_qa.r: Boyd uses sports analogies frequently in his leadership approach, viewing the team dynamic with customers as similar to athletes striving for common purpose. He emphasizes that improvement is about getting one rep in daily and being better than yesterday, building muscle over time. He also references Ted Lasso's leadership philosophy in a presentation he developed, connecting coaching principles to safety management and technology adoption.
